q: Do I have to answer police questions or attend an interview in NSW?
a: Under NSW law, you have a fundamental common law and statutory right to silence. Aside from providing your name, residential address, and driver licence (if driving), you are not legally required to answer questions, participate in an electronically recorded interview (ERISP), or explain your side of the story. In fact, answering police questions without legal advice is one of the most common mistakes individuals make, as casual remarks or partial explanations can be taken out of context and used against you in court. Contact Adam Ashley immediately before saying anything to police.

q: Can police search my vehicle without a warrant on the side of the road?
a: Under Section 36 of the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW) (LEPRA), police can search a vehicle without a warrant only if they hold "reasonable suspicion" that the car contains stolen goods, illicit drugs, dangerous weapons (such as guns or knives), or implements intended for an offence. A hunch or random traffic stop does not legally suffice. If police lack genuine reasonable suspicion, any evidence seized may be deemed illegally obtained and excluded under Section 138 of the Evidence Act. We routinely challenge unlawful police vehicle searches.

q: Can police search my mobile phone or force me to hand over my passcode/PIN?
a: Generally, police cannot force you to unlock your phone, provide your PIN code, or scan your face/fingerprint upon a routine street arrest or stop-and-search without a specific digital search warrant or an auxiliary order under federal legislation (such as a 3LA Order under the Crimes Act 1914 for Commonwealth matters). In NSW state matters, you are not required to give up your passcode merely because police ask. Always politely state that you wish to consult criminal lawyer Adam Ashley before complying with device access demands.

q: Can police strip search me just because a drug sniffer dog sits next to me?
a: In NSW, under the LEPRA framework, a drug detection dog's indication alone does not automatically establish reasonable suspicion justifying an intrusive strip search. While police use a canine indication as grounds for a general search (emptying pockets and bags), strict statutory safeguards govern when strip searches may occur (requiring seriousness and urgency under Section 31 LEPRA). Unlawful strip searches at music festivals, train stations, or pubs are frequently challenged in court to have evidence thrown out under Section 138 of the Evidence Act.

q: How long can NSW police detain me after an arrest before charging or releasing me?
a: Under Part 9 of LEPRA, police may detain an arrested person for an "investigation period" of up to 6 hours. However, police can apply to an authorised magistrate or judicial officer for a detention warrant extending this period by up to an additional 6 hours. Crucially, "time-out" periods (such as time spent waiting for legal advice from your lawyer, medical attention, or an interpreter) do not count toward the 6-hour limit. If you are detained in the cells, assert your right to contact Frontline Lawyers immediately.

q: When is a police arrest considered unlawful under Section 99 LEPRA in NSW?
a: Section 99 of the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 sets strict limits on arrest without warrant. Police cannot arrest you simply to interview you, question you, or investigate suspicions when issuing a Court Attendance Notice (can) would suffice. They must satisfy a two-part test: (1) suspecting on reasonable grounds that you committed an offence, and (2) establishing that arrest is strictly necessary for specific statutory reasons (e.g., stopping fleeing, ensuring court appearance, or protecting evidence). Unlawful arrests can result in charges being dismissed and civil claims for compensation.

q: What should I do if police knock on my door with a search warrant (raid)?
a: First, request to inspect the search warrant before allowing entry. Confirm the address listed, verify that it is signed and dated by an authorised justice, and note the specific items police are authorised to search for. You are not required to answer informal questions or participate in an interview during the execution of the warrant. Contact Frontline Lawyers immediately so our defence team can monitor the search, object to unlawful seizures, and protect privileged documents.

q: What happens if I blew over the limit or got caught drink driving (DUI) in NSW?
a: In NSW, drink driving offences (PCA offences under the Road Transport Act 2013) carry immediate police licence suspensions, mandatory disqualification periods, substantial fines, and mandatory Alcohol Interlock orders. Offence brackets range from Novice/Special Range (over 0.00 or 0.02), Low Range (0.05 to 0.079), Mid Range (0.08 to 0.149), to High Range (0.150 and above). For Mid and High Range, the court may also consider custodial sentences unless strong mitigation and rehabilitation are presented by an experienced defence lawyer.

q: Can I be charged with drug driving if I have a legal medical weed prescription?
a: Yes. Under Section 111 of the Road Transport Act 2013 (NSW), it is an offence to drive with any detectable presence of illicit drugs (including THC/cannabis) in your oral fluid, blood, or urine. Unlike other states like Tasmania, NSW law currently does not provide an automatic statutory defence or exemption for legally prescribed medicinal cannabis patients. Even if you consumed medicinal cannabis days earlier and are completely unimpaired, a positive roadside tongue swipe can trigger prosecution. Adam Ashley provides expert defence representation to protect your licence.

q: What are the penalties for High-Range Drink Driving (0.150+) in NSW?
a: High-Range PCA (BAC 0.150 or higher) is treated as an extremely serious criminal offence in NSW. For a first offence, penalties include a maximum fine of $3,300, up to 18 months imprisonment, an automatic licence disqualification of 3 years (minimum 12 months), and a mandatory 24-month Alcohol Interlock Order. For a second or subsequent major offence within 5 years, maximum prison time increases to 2 years with a minimum 4-year interlock period. Urgent legal representation is essential to argue for non-custodial sentences and reduced disqualification.

q: How does the mandatory Alcohol Interlock Program work in NSW?
a: The NSW Mandatory Alcohol Interlock Program requires drivers convicted of Mid-Range PCA, High-Range PCA, or repeat drink driving offences to install an electronic breath-testing device wired to their car's ignition. The vehicle will not start if alcohol is detected on the driver's breath. You must serve a minimum court-ordered disqualification period before obtaining an Interlock Licence for 12 to 48 months. Under Section 212 of the Road Transport Act, Adam Ashley can apply for an Interlock Exemption Order if severe medical or economic hardship is proven.

q: What happens if I refuse a roadside breath test or station breath analysis?
a: Refusing or failing to submit to a roadside breath test, or refusing to provide a breath sample for analysis at the police station, is treated under NSW law as seriously as a High-Range PCA charge. It carries severe penalties including immediate licence suspension, substantial fines, mandatory interlock orders, and potential prison time. Unless you have a genuine medical inability to blow (supported by specialist medical evidence), refusal is rarely advantageous.

q: Can I appeal an immediate police roadside licence suspension notice?
a: Yes. If police issue an on-the-spot licence suspension notice for drink driving or excessive speeding (exceeding speed limit by over 30km/h or 45km/h), you have 28 days to lodge a Licence Suspension Appeal in the Local Court. You must satisfy the magistrate that "exceptional circumstances" exist to justify lifting the suspension pending the final determination of the charge. We prepare detailed evidentiary briefs establishing urgent employment, medical, or family necessity.

q: What are the penalties for driving while disqualified or suspended in NSW?
a: Driving while disqualified is viewed by NSW courts as a direct defiance of a court order. Penalties include automatic further disqualification periods, substantial fines of up to $3,300, and up to 6 months imprisonment for a first offence (or 12 months for repeat offences). For suspended driving (e.g. unpaid fines or demerit points), penalties are also significant. Experienced representation is essential to argue for community-based sentencing or dismissal.

q: What does "Show Cause" mean under the NSW Bail Act 2013?
a: Under Section 16A of the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), if you are charged with a "show cause offence" (such as serious commercial drug supply, aggravated sexual assault, firearms offences, armed robbery, or serious violent offences), the court must refuse bail unless the accused person shows cause why their detention is not justified. This is a reverse legal burden. Adam Ashley crafts rigorous show cause submissions demonstrating compelling factors like strength of defence, young age, medical needs, delay, or an unblemished record.

q: What is the "Unacceptable Risk" test used by magistrates when deciding bail?
a: Even if show cause is satisfied (or for non-show-cause offences), the court must assess whether there is an unacceptable risk that the accused person will: (1) fail to appear at court, (2) commit a serious offence while on bail, (3) endanger the safety of victims or the community, or (4) interfere with witnesses or evidence. Bail conditions (such as curfews, daily reporting, sureties, and non-association orders) are designed to mitigate these risks to an acceptable level.

q: Can I apply for bail a second time in the Local Court if my first application was refused?
a: Under Section 74 of the NSW Bail Act, you cannot make a second bail application in the same court unless you demonstrate a "change of circumstances" or that material information was not presented at the first hearing. This makes the initial bail application critical. If bail was refused in the Local Court, your primary remedy is an urgent application to the Supreme Court of NSW in Sydney.

q: What happens at a Weekend Bail Court via Audio Visual Link (AVL)?
a: If you are arrested on a Friday night, weekend, or public holiday in the Northern Rivers (e.g. Tweed, Byron, or Lismore), police will hold you in cells and list your matter before the centralized Weekend Bail Court (often Parramatta Bail Court or regional AVL hub). The hearing takes place by Audio Visual Link. Having a private defence lawyer appear remotely or via agent ensures that detailed bail material, surety verification, and residential addresses are properly presented to the magistrate.

q: What is an "acceptable person" or surety in a criminal bail application?
a: A surety (or "acceptable person") is an individual—usually a family member or close friend—who agrees to deposit or forfeit a sum of money or equity in property if the accused person breaches bail and fails to appear in court. The court reviews the surety's character, criminal record, financial standing, and relationship with the accused to ensure the guarantee is genuine and influential.

q: What should I do if police allege I breached my bail conditions in NSW?
a: If police suspect a bail breach (e.g., missing curfew by minutes, failing to report, or returning a positive breath test), they have power to arrest you under Section 77 of the Bail Act and bring you before court. At court, the magistrate has discretion to take no action, release you on the same bail, vary your conditions, or revoke bail entirely. Adam Ashley acts rapidly to explain administrative oversights or emergencies to prevent clients from being remanded in custody.

q: What happens if you get into a fight, pub brawl, or scrap in NSW?
a: Physical altercations at licensed premises, clubs, or on the street are prosecuted vigorously in NSW. Charges range from Common Assault (Section 61 Crimes Act - max 2 years) to Affray (Section 93C Crimes Act - using or threatening unlawful violence causing a person of reasonable firmness to fear for safety - max 10 years). If injuries occur, charges elevate to Assault Occasioning Actual Bodily Harm (AOABH - max 5 to 7 years) or Wounding/GBH. Defence preparation looks closely at CCTV footage, security staff statements and any self-defence evidence.

q: What is the legal difference between Common Assault, AOABH, Wounding, and GBH?
a: NSW criminal law grades assaults according to intent and severity of injury: Common Assault (s61 Crimes Act) involves threats or physical force causing no injury or fleeting discomfort (max 2 years); Assault Occasioning Actual Bodily Harm - AOABH (s59) involves injuries that interfere with health or comfort, like cuts or bruising (max 5 years); Wounding or Grievous Bodily Harm - GBH (s33, s35) involves breaking all layers of skin or really serious permanent bodily harm (max up to 25 years). The charge grade dictates whether the case is finalised in the Local Court or goes to a jury trial in the District Court.

q: Can I claim self-defence if I hit or punched someone first during an altercation?
a: Yes. Under Section 418 of the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW), pre-emptive force can be lawful self-defence if you genuinely believed an imminent attack was about to occur. The legal test is: (1) Did the accused genuinely believe their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another person? (Subjective test), and (2) Was their conduct a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them? (Objective test). Once evidence of self-defence is raised, the prosecution bears the heavy burden of disproving it beyond reasonable doubt.

q: Can the police proceed with an assault charge if the alleged victim wants to drop it?
a: Yes. In NSW, criminal charges are brought by the State (the NSW Police Force or Director of Public Prosecutions), not the private individual. Even if the complainant signs a formal retraction statement or refuses to attend court, police can and often do proceed using triple-zero (000) audio recordings, body-worn video (BWV) footage, and medical records.

q: What is the difference between an ADVO (Domestic) and an APVO (Personal)?
a: An Apprehended Domestic Violence Order (ADVO) is made between individuals who have had a domestic relationship (spouses, de facto partners, ex-partners, family members, or flatmates). An Apprehended Personal Violence Order (APVO) involves individuals who are not related (such as disputing neighbours, co-workers, or strangers). While an AVO itself is a civil order and not an initial criminal conviction, any alleged breach of an AVO is a serious criminal offence under Section 14 of the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 carrying up to 2 years imprisonment.

q: What happens if I breach an AVO by sending a text message or phone call to my ex?
a: In NSW, under Section 14 of the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007, knowingly contravening an AVO—even via a single text message, email, social media DM, or asking a third party to send a message—is a criminal offence punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment and a $5,500 fine. Furthermore, if the breach involves an act of violence, Section 14(4) creates a statutory presumption that the court must impose a full-time prison sentence unless exceptional reasons exist.

q: Should I contest an AVO or consent "Without Admissions" in the Local Court?
a: Consenting to an AVO "without admission of liability" resolves the civil order without a formal finding that you committed domestic violence. However, accepting an AVO triggers immediate consequences: automatic revocation of firearms licences for 10 years, potential impacts on working with children checks or security clearances, and vulnerability to criminal breach charges. If the allegations are fabricated or exaggerated, Adam Ashley regularly defends and defeats contested AVO hearings.

q: Can police immediately exclude me from my home using a provisional ADVO (kicked out)?
a: Yes. NSW Police can make an urgent Provisional ADVO with an exclusion condition prohibiting you from approaching or entering the family residence, even if you are the sole owner, titleholder, or leaseholder. Once served, entering the property constitutes a criminal breach. Adam Ashley can make an urgent variation application to the Local Court to challenge unreasonable exclusion orders and negotiate property access protocols.

q: What happens if police catch me with weed (cannabis) or personal gear in NSW?
a: Under Section 10 of the Drug Misuse and Trafficking Act 1985 (NSW), possessing any quantity of an illicit drug is a criminal offence carrying penalties of up to 2 years imprisonment and a $2,200 fine. However, for minor first-time cannabis possession (under 15 grams), police may exercise discretion under the Cannabis Cautioning Scheme. If the matter goes to court, outcomes such as a Section 10 dismissal or a Conditional Release Order without conviction may be available, depending on your circumstances.

q: What happens if police catch you with personal gear, ice, coke, or pills?
a: Possession of prohibited drugs such as methylamphetamine (ice / gear / shard), cocaine (coke / rack / bags), or MDMA (ecstasy / caps / pills) is prosecuted under Section 10 of the DMTA. While classified as summary matters in the Local Court for personal use quantities, magistrates take hard drugs seriously. Defences focus on whether you had legal knowledge and exclusive physical control, whether the search was lawful under LEPRA, or preparing comprehensive rehabilitation material to achieve a non-conviction outcome.

q: What is "Deemed Supply" and when does having gear or pills become dealing in NSW?
a: In NSW, under Section 29 of the Drug Misuse and Trafficking Act, if you are found possessing a quantity of drugs at or above the "trafficable quantity" threshold (e.g., 3 grams of cocaine, 3 grams of MDMA/caps, or 300 grams of cannabis), the law automatically presumes you possessed them for commercial supply. The burden of proof shifts to the accused to prove on the balance of probabilities that the substances were exclusively for personal consumption. Forensic analysis, purity testing, and expert evidence are vital to defeat deemed supply.

q: What is the NSW Cannabis Cautioning Scheme and who qualifies?
a: Under the NSW Police Cannabis Cautioning Scheme, police have discretion to issue a formal caution rather than charging you with an offence if you are found in possession of not more than 15 grams of cannabis for personal use. To qualify, you must be an adult, have no prior convictions for drug offences or violent crimes, and admit to the possession. You can receive a maximum of two cautions in a lifetime before criminal charges become mandatory.

q: What is the MERIT Program and can it help me avoid a criminal sentence?
a: The Magistrates Early Referral Into Treatment (MERIT) program is a specialized court diversion program available in NSW Local Courts for eligible defendants with substance use issues. Participation is voluntary and lasts approximately 12 weeks while your court proceedings are adjourned. Successfully completing MERIT provides powerful mitigation at sentencing, frequently enabling magistrates to impose non-conviction orders (CROs) or avoid custodial penalties.

q: What are the penalties for Commercial and Large Commercial Drug Supply in NSW?
a: Commercial Quantity and Large Commercial Quantity supply are strictly indictable charges prosecuted by the DPP in the District or Supreme Court. Large Commercial Supply carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment and substantial standard non-parole periods (ranging from 10 to 15 years). Defending these charges requires rigorous scrutiny of telecommunications warrants, electronic surveillance, undercover operatives, and supply chain evidence.

q: Can I be charged with drug possession if illicit substances were found in a shared house?
a: Yes, police often charge everyone on the premises when drugs are discovered in shared spaces like living rooms, kitchen cupboards, or shared cars. However, under the leading High Court authority He Kaw Teh and NSW case law (such as Filipetti), the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that you had both physical custody/control and actual knowledge of the existence and illicit nature of the drug. If drugs were in a common area accessible to multiple housemates or visitors, proving who possessed them can be difficult for the prosecution.

q: What are the penalties for possessing an unregistered gun or unlicensed firearm?
a: Under the Firearms Act 1996 (NSW), possessing an unauthorised or unregistered firearm (including rifles, shotguns, handguns, and pistols) is treated with extreme severity. Possessing an unregistered firearm (Section 36) carries up to 5 years imprisonment in the Local/District Court. Possessing an unauthorised pistol or prohibited firearm (Section 7A) carries up to 14 years imprisonment, with strict mandatory sentencing provisions for commercial supply or possessing multiple firearms (Section 51D). Even holding an inherited gun without a licence is a criminal offence. Frontline Lawyers provides specialized firearm defence representation.

q: Are gel blasters, replica guns, or BB guns illegal in NSW?
a: Yes. In New South Wales, gel blasters, airsoft guns, and replica firearms that closely resemble functioning firearms are legally classified as "imitation firearms" or "prohibited weapons" under the Firearms Act 1996 and Weapons Prohibition Act 1998. It is an offence to possess or use a gel blaster without a specific firearms permit or legitimate prohibited weapon permit. Penalties can mirror those for possessing a genuine firearm. If you have been charged after ordering a gel blaster online or possessing one recreationally, speak to Adam Ashley immediately.

q: What are the NSW laws for storing firearms and ammunition safely?
a: Under Part 4 of the Firearms Act 1996, licence holders are held to strict statutory storage standards: Category A and B firearms must be stored in an approved steel gun safe (or solid timber safe) bolted to the structure, with ammunition stored in a separate locked receptacle. Category C, D, and H (pistols) require safes of specified steel thickness and compliant alarm systems. Police conduct random audits, and failing to comply can lead to criminal charges under Section 39, seizure of all firearms, and permanent licence cancellation.

q: Is it illegal to carry a pocket knife, box cutter, or blade in NSW?
a: Under Section 11C of the Summary Offences Act 1988 (NSW), it is an offence to possess a knife in a public place or school without a "reasonable excuse". While lawful occupation (tradesperson carrying tools for work), food preparation, or legitimate recreation (fishing or scouting) are recognised excuses, self-defence is explicitly not a legal excuse. Recent legislative reforms have granted police expanded powers to search individuals for knives, blades, and weapons without a warrant in designated entertainment precincts.

q: What is considered a "prohibited weapon" under NSW law (tasers, knuckle dusters)?
a: Under Schedule 1 of the Weapons Prohibition Act 1998 (NSW), prohibited weapons include flick knives, butterfly knives, brass knuckles (knuckle dusters), tasers / stun devices, pepper spray / mace, extendable batons, and crossbows. Possessing an unauthorised prohibited weapon carries up to 14 years imprisonment. If you face weapons charges, Frontline Lawyers investigates classification issues, import permits, and collectors exemptions.

q: How do criminal charges or AVOs affect my NSW firearms licence (seized guns)?
a: Under the Firearms Act 1996 (NSW), the NSW Firearms Registry has strict statutory obligations: if an interim or final AVO is made against you, your firearms licence is automatically suspended or revoked, and police will seize all registered firearms and ammunition. Furthermore, convictions for violence or drug offences result in a mandatory 10-year statutory ban on holding a licence. We assist primary producers, sports shooters, and security personnel with Firearms Appeals in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT).

q: What is the legal difference between Larceny, Shoplifting, and Stealing in NSW?
a: Larceny (Section 117 Crimes Act) occurs when a person takes and carries away personal property belonging to another without consent, intending to permanently deprive the owner. Shoplifting (nicking or pinching retail goods) is standard larceny carrying up to 5 years (or 2 years in Local Court). Stealing by Clerk or Servant / Embezzlement (Section 156 Crimes Act) involves an employee misappropriating money or goods entrusted to them, carrying a maximum penalty of 10 years due to the breach of fiduciary trust.

q: What is the difference between NSW state fraud and Commonwealth fraud (Centrelink/ATO)?
a: NSW state fraud (Section 192E Crimes Act) involves dishonestly obtaining financial advantage or causing financial disadvantage by deception, carrying up to 10 years imprisonment. Commonwealth fraud charges (under the Criminal Code 1995 (Cth)) relate to federal institutions, including Centrelink, the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), Medicare, NDIS, or international banking transactions. Commonwealth offences are prosecuted by the CDPP and involve stringent federal sentencing guidelines.

q: Can the police or Crime Commission freeze my bank accounts and assets before trial?
a: Yes. Under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (Cth) or the Criminal Assets Recovery Act 1990 (NSW), authorities such as the NSW Crime Commission (NSWCC) or Australian Federal Police (AFP) can obtain restraining orders freezing bank accounts, luxury vehicles, and real estate, even before criminal guilt has been proven. Urgent legal action is required to apply for living expenses, legal defence allowances, and exclusions of legitimate assets.

q: What penalties apply for identity theft and cyber fraud in NSW?
a: Identity fraud offences under Part 4AB of the Crimes Act 1900 carry up to 10 years imprisonment for possessing, producing, or using false identification information with intent to commit an indictable offence. Federal cyber crime provisions under the Criminal Code 1995 (Cth) target unauthorised access, computer modification, and business email compromise (BEC). We work with forensic cyber specialists to examine server logs and digital chains of custody.

q: Can charges be withdrawn or downgraded before a hearing?
a: In many criminal matters, cases can be resolved without ever going to a defended hearing. Adam Ashley conducts detailed evidentiary audits of the police brief of evidence to identify weaknesses in the evidence, unlawful police searches under LEPRA, or unreliable witness statements. We then draft formal Written Legal Representations to the Police Area Commander or Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), petitioning for charges to be formally withdrawn, dismissed, or negotiated down to lesser summary offences.

q: Can I avoid a criminal record in NSW?
a: Yes. Under Section 10 of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999, a court can find an offence proven but dismiss the charge without recording a criminal conviction. Alternatively, under Section 9(1)(b), the court can impose a Conditional Release Order (CRO) without conviction for up to 2 years. Factors magistrates weigh include: your prior clean record, age, mental health, remorse, the trivial nature of the offence, and the severe employment or travel impact a conviction would trigger. Frontline Lawyers has an exceptional track record achieving non-conviction outcomes.

q: What is the difference between the Local Court and District Court of NSW?
a: The Local Court handles summary offences (such as drink driving, minor assaults, and small drug possession) and table offences, presided over by a magistrate without a jury. Its jurisdictional sentencing limit is generally 2 years per offence (or 5 years cumulative). The District Court hears appeals from the Local Court and serious indictable charges (such as commercial drug supply, manslaughter, serious sexual assault, and robbery) before a judge and jury, with significantly higher sentencing powers.

q: What is a Section 14 Mental Health Diversion (formerly Section 32)?
a: Under Section 14 of the Mental Health and Cognitive Impairment Forensic Provisions Act 2020 (NSW), a magistrate can dismiss your criminal charges without a conviction or finding of guilt on the condition that you participate in a mental health or psychological treatment plan. To succeed, we obtain expert forensic psychological or psychiatric reports establishing a diagnosis (e.g. PTSD, depression, ADHD, substance disorder) and drafting an enforceable treatment plan showing treatment is more appropriate than punitive sentencing.

q: What sentencing discount do I receive for an early guilty plea in NSW?
a: Under the statutory sentencing discount scheme (Part 3 Division 1A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999), an early guilty plea entered in the Local Court at the committal stage provides a mandatory 25% discount on your sentence (including prison terms or community service). If entered later in the District Court, the discount drops to 10% or 5%. Strategic timing of pleas can make the difference between serving time or remaining in the community.

q: What is an Intensive Correction Order (ICO) and can it keep me out of prison (jail)?
a: An Intensive Correction Order (ICO) under Section 7 of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 is a term of imprisonment of up to 2 years served in the community under strict supervision, rather than inside a correctional centre. Mandatory conditions include not committing offences, alongside potential conditions like community service work, curfews, electronic monitoring, alcohol bans, or rehabilitation. Community safety is the paramount consideration.

q: How do I appeal an unfair Local Court sentence to the District Court?
a: You have an automatic right of appeal under the Crimes (Appeal and Review) Act 2001 to appeal a Local Court sentence (Severity Appeal) or conviction (All-Grounds Appeal) to the District Court within 28 days of sentencing (or up to 3 months with court leave). The District Court judge hears the matter afresh. If the judge is contemplating a more severe penalty than the magistrate imposed, they must give a "Parker Warning", allowing you to withdraw the appeal.

q: What is a Pre-Sentence Report (Sentencing Assessment Report) from Community Corrections?
a: A Sentencing Assessment Report (SAR) is an objective report ordered by the magistrate or judge and prepared by NSW Community Corrections officers before sentencing. They interview you to evaluate your risk of reoffending, suitability for community work or an Intensive Correction Order (ICO), and attitude toward the offence. Performing well in this interview is crucial, as an unfavorable report often leads magistrates to conclude that prison is the only viable sentence.

q: How should character references be written for a NSW criminal court hearing?
a: Effective character references can substantially alter sentencing outcomes. A reference must be typed, dated, signed, and addressed to "The Presiding Magistrate" or "The Presiding Judge". Crucially, the referee must state that they know about your specific criminal charges and are aware of your plea. They should outline your good character, work ethic, community contribution, and remorse without lecturing the court on what penalty to impose. We provide custom reference guideline templates to our clients.

q: When does a criminal conviction become "spent" and disappear from my record in NSW?
a: Under the Criminal Records Act 1991 (NSW), most Local Court convictions become "spent" after a 10-year crime-free period for adult offences (or 3 years for juvenile matters), meaning you generally do not need to disclose them for standard employment. However, certain convictions never become spent (such as prison sentences over 6 months or sexual offences), and exemptions exist for law enforcement, judicial, working with children, and security roles.

a: Yes. Many individuals visiting Byron Bay, Tweed Heads, or Northern Rivers from Brisbane, Gold Coast, Sydney, or Melbourne find themselves charged under NSW laws. Because NSW criminal law differs significantly from Queensland and other states, having experienced a NSW criminal defence lawyer is essential. We can manage your initial mentions remotely, obtain the police brief, and represent you in court so your travel is minimised.
